entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC), officially published in 1992 by the Vatican, serves as a comprehensive exposition of Catholic doctrine and teachings. This monumental text, developed under the direction of Pope John Paul II, encapsulates the beliefs and practices of the Roman Catholic Church, addressing doctrinal points in a systematic manner. It is not merely a book but a pivotal reference for Catholics worldwide, influencing the Church's educational programs and theological discourse since its release. Its impact extends beyond ecclesiastical boundaries, reflecting broader historical currents in modern Christianity and shaping the faith of millions across diverse cultures and contexts.

The Catechism emerged from the post-Vatican II Church's need for a clear and accessible presentation of Catholic faith, which arose from the Second Vatican Council held between 1962 and 1965. The council called for renewal in the Church’s engagement with contemporary society, leading to a more dialogical and catechetical approach. The CCC synthesizes Scripture, Tradition, and the teachings of the Church Fathers, compiling insights from various Church documents and papal encyclicals into a cohesive format. Its structure, divided into four main parts—The Profession of Faith, The Celebration of the Christian Mystery, Life in Christ, and Christian Prayer—provides a thorough educational framework for understanding Catholicism.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Catechism of the Catholic Church (Latin: Catechismus Catholicae Ecclesiae) is the official compendium of Catholic doctrine and teaching, promulgated by Pope John Paul II on 11 October 1992 — the thirtieth anniversary of the opening of the Second Vatican Council — and published in its definitive edition (the editio typica) in Latin in 1997. It is the first universal catechism since the Roman Catechism (Catechismus Romanus) promulgated after the Council of Trent in 1566 — four centuries previously — and reflects the teaching of Vatican II while presenting the whole of Catholic doctrine in a systematic, accessible form intended for the universal Church. Comprising 2,865 numbered paragraphs organized in four 'pillars' (The Creed; The Sacraments; The Commandments; and Prayer), the Catechism covers the entirety of Catholic belief and moral teaching, from the doctrine of the Trinity and Christology through the seven sacraments, through the moral theology of the commandments (including the Church's positions on abortion, contraception, capital punishment, war, social justice, and sexuality), to a systematic treatment of prayer culminating in the Our Father.

The Catechism was initiated at the Extraordinary Synod of Bishops (1985) called to evaluate the reception of Vatican II twenty years after its conclusion, and produced by a commission of twelve cardinals and bishops chaired by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger (later Pope Benedict XVI) over six years of drafting (1986–1992). Its promulgation under John Paul II — who wrote a special Apostolic Constitution (Fidei Depositum) for its presentation — was a major moment in the pontificate, consolidating the interpretation of Vatican II in a way that both welcomed the Council's renewal and resisted more radical post-conciliar interpretations.

The Catechism has been translated into more than forty languages and has sold tens of millions of copies worldwide — the best-selling catechism in the history of the Catholic Church.
